extracted.intended_audience: secondary-school students and coaches preparing for math olympiads
extracted.subtask_description: Solution techniques and proof-strategies for China Mathematical Olympiad problems (number theory, combinatorics, geometry, inequalities, recurrences). Focus is on how to produce/structure correct contest solutions using classical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine closed-form of sequence and observe monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a property like (1) it is mainly required to determine the expression of a_n; its monotonicity can be observed directly from the expression of a_n. (Some students pointed out that a_n > a_{n+1} is obvious after writing down the expression of a_n.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find an explicit formula for the sequence term a_n (or a convenient closed form). Once the expression is obtained monotonicity (or other termwise inequalities) should be checked directly from that expression rather than by ad hoc comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inclusion–exclusion to count elements divisible by small primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Define T_n = { t | t < n+1 and 2 | t or 3 | t } (or analogous sets) and apply the inclusion–exclusion principle to compute |T_n| and hence bound quantities like f(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When counting numbers in a block that are divisible by given primes, compute counts by inclusion–exclusion (counts divisible by 2 plus by 3 minus by 6, etc.) and then relate that count to the combinatorial quantity of interest (e.g. maximal subset avoiding 3 mutually prime elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct 'bad' subset (e.g. numbers divisible by 2 or 3) to give lower/upper bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a subset T_n (for example numbers divisible by 2 or 3) such that any 3 elements in T_n are not mutually prime, so from that observation derive bounds like f(n) ≥ |T_n| + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove lower bounds on the minimal size required to guarantee a property, explicitly construct large subsets that avoid the property (anti-examples). Use their size to deduce lower bounds; conversely, use complementary counting to obtain upper bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove small base cases by parity and divisibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify base values (e.g. f(4)=4, f(5)=5, f(6)=5) by analyzing parities and divisibility by small primes (2,3,5) in consecutive integer sets and checking which 3-element subsets can/cannot be mutually prime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small n, exhaust possible parity distributions (counts of odd/even) and check divisibility by small primes across the chosen elements; use this to demonstrate existence/nonexistence of 3 mutually prime elements and thus determine exact f(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extend formulas by mathematical induction using block decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a general formula for f(n) by induction: divide the n-length interval into blocks (e.g. blocks of length 6) and consider residues r to handle all cases; use previously established values for smaller n and combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition the set of consecutive integers into equal-size blocks (often related to the lcm of small primes, here 6) and handle residues separately. Use induction hypothesis on sub-blocks and combine inequalities to deduce the result for the next sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Pigeonhole Principle to force existence in grouped arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: When numbers are partitioned into K groups of size 6 plus r leftover, counting elements ensures at least one group contains sufficiently many elements (e.g. 5) so previously computed values (like f(6)=5) can be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After grouping elements, count how many chosen elements must fall into the groups; if average exceeds threshold, deduce existence of a group meeting the threshold and apply known small-case results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct auxiliary circle and use concyclicity and angle-chasing to locate incenter
rubrics_metrics.description: Given triangle ABC and AD = AC, construct circle centered at A with radius AC intersecting AB at D and a line I at E,F; then show DE passes through the incenter by joining DE, DC, drawing angle bisectors and demonstrating concyclicity and equal angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use auxiliary constructions (circum/central circles, angle bisectors) to produce cyclic quadrilaterals; then perform angle chasing to identify equal angles that imply a point is the incenter (or lies on an angle bisector). Explicit equal-length or perpendicular relations often yield concyclicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external angle bisectors and cyclic quadrilaterals to locate excenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend FD to meet the bisector of the exterior angle and use cyclicity and right-angle relations to show the point of intersection is an excenter (escenter) of triangle ABC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine properties of angle bisectors (internal and external), cyclic quadrilaterals, and right-angle relations to prove collinearity or that a constructed point satisfies the defining properties of an excenter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate algebraic constraints to a triangle/cosine model to simplify minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Given positive a,b,c,x,y,z with relations like cz + bz = a etc., observe that b^2+... inequalities imply the existence of an acute triangle with sides a,b,c and set x = cos A, y = cos B, z = cos C; then reduce the target function to one in cosines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When symmetric algebraic relations suggest trigonometric identities (e.g. expressions of the form u^2+v^2+w^2 and uv+vw+wu), attempt to interpret variables as cosines/cotangents of triangle angles to leverage known triangle identities and simplify optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cotangent substitution and sum-of-squares decomposition to get sharp inequality bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Set u = cot A, v = cot B, w = cot C so that uv+vw+wu = 1 and express the target as a sum that can be bounded below via sum-of-squares or rearrangement; equality occurs at u = v = w (equilateral triangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After substituting, manipulate the expression into sums of nonnegative terms (e.g. u^2+v^2+w^2 minus symmetric combinations) to obtain lower bounds; identify when equality holds by symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting via grid/table and divisor-function sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Place stars at grid positions where a position is a multiple of its row index in a 2k x 2k table; count total stars by rows (summing [2k/i]) and by columns (summing divisor counts T(j)), equate counts to derive sums involving divisor functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-counting arguments on structured grids are useful: count the same set in two different ways (by rows and by columns) to link arithmetic functions like floor(2k/i) and divisor-count sums T(j). Use these equalities to compute specific totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit lattice-point parity and minimal-area arguments for integer-coordinate configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: In a set of integer-coordinate points forming polygons, two vertices must share parity class; their midpoint is an integer point. Use a minimal-area convex pentagon argument to deduce the midpoint lies on an edge and derive contradictions, forcing existence of interior lattice points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partition lattice points by (x mod 2, y mod 2) classes; midpoints of same-class pairs are lattice points. Combine with minimal-area arguments (areas of integer polygons are multiples of 1/2) to get contradictions or produce required interior points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Menelaus' theorem and parallelisms to relate segment ratios in quadrilateral configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: When several quadrilaterals/segments are in parallel correspondence (e.g. ElF1 // EF etc.), use Menelaus' theorem on appropriate triangles/lines to derive equalities of ratios and consequently express a desired ratio (or angle expression) in terms of a given parameter A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify transversals and triangles where Menelaus' theorem applies. Use the given parallelisms to convert segment ratios along transversals into known proportions, then algebraically manipulate to get the target expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve recurrences with floor by decomposing into polynomial/modular components
rubrics_metrics.description: For sequences defined by x_{n+1} = xn + [ (n+2)^2 / 4 ] or similar involving floors, decompose into components u_n, y_n, z_n based on residues (e.g. mod 3) and express x_n in closed form depending on n and initial c modulo classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split the sequence into simpler additive sequences (polynomial parts and residue-dependent parts). Identify periodic or modular behavior (e.g. every 3 terms) and derive explicit formulas for each residue class, then combine to get full closed form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove uniqueness of constructed sequence via maximum-difference contraction
rubrics_metrics.description: To show uniqueness of a sequence satisfying a linear relation (e.g. xi+1 = 2 xi + 2a^3 - xi-1), assume two solutions and consider the index where the absolute difference is largest; show a contraction (strict inequality) leading to contradiction unless differences are zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a sup-norm / maximum-index argument: pick i maximizing |w_i - v_i|, derive an inequality showing the maximum must decrease (or be zero), and hence conclude all differences vanish and sequences coincide.
